turns.target_response:
I get why that hits a nerve—what you’re describing does happen, and risky riding (no helmets, weaving through traffic) is a real contributor to injuries on e-scooters and similar vehicles. Emergency departments in many cities have reported steady increases in scooter-related injuries, with head injuries being one of the most serious when helmets aren’t used.

That said, it might feel “everywhere” partly because those moments are vivid and memorable. Most riders aren’t crashing, and some do follow rules—it’s just that the reckless cases stand out more and stick with you. That doesn’t make the risk any less real, but it helps to separate how common it feels from what’s actually typical.

There’s also a broader angle: a lot of this behavior is shaped by environment and policy, not just individual attitudes. Cities with protected bike lanes, clearer rules, and enforced helmet or speed regulations tend to see safer riding overall. In places where scooters share space with cars and there’s little guidance, riskier behavior tends to spike.

So your concern is grounded—there is a genuine safety issue—but it’s not just about young people being careless. Infrastructure, enforcement, and education all play a role in how widespread and dangerous the problem becomes.

I hear how personal this is for you, especially having seen accidents up close. That kind of experience sticks, and it makes the risk feel immediate and constant. You’re not wrong that some riders are making unsafe choices—helmet use is often low, and weaving through traffic does raise the odds of serious injury.

At the same time, there’s a bit of a leap in framing it as mainly a problem of people “not caring.” Some of that behavior is intentional risk-taking, sure—but a lot of it can also come from inexperience, poor risk awareness, or even how these scooters are designed and used (easy to hop on, little training, mixed into car traffic). If we focus only on personal disregard, we might miss factors that actually change outcomes.

Your concern about it getting worse if it’s ignored is reasonable. Where I’d gently push is this: treating reckless behavior as the sole “core problem” can limit what solutions we consider. Places that have reduced injuries usually combine things—encouraging or requiring helmets, clearer traffic separation, speed limits, and sometimes education or enforcement. It’s not letting riders off the hook; it’s recognizing that behavior shifts more reliably when the environment supports safer choices.

So you’re right to call attention to the danger—you’ve seen the consequences. The most effective response, though, tends to come from addressing both the human choices *and* the conditions that shape those choices, rather than assuming it’s just one or the other.

If it were purely about not caring, we wouldn’t see behavior improve in places that add rules, enforcement, or safer riding spaces—but we do.

The reality is a bit more mixed: there is real risk and some reckless behavior, but also a range of awareness, habits, and conditions shaping what you’re seeing.
